(p-336) Surah al-Tawbah (p-336) is Medinan according to all of them.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) Surah Bara'ah was called al-Fadiha (the Disgracer), because it exposed the hypocrites.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq related that in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) it was called al-Mubaʿthirah (the Scatterer), because of what it uncovered of the secrets of the people. It is Medinan according to all of them.

Muqatil alone said: "Except for the last two verses, ﴿Indeed there has come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], which were revealed in Mecca."

﴿A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists.﴾ ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months, and know that you cannot escape Allah, and that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers.﴾

As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists﴾, regarding the omission of the basmalah (﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾) at the beginning of this surah, there are two opinions. The first: this surah and al-Anfal are like a single surah in subject matter, because the first deals with the mention of covenants and the second with the cancellation of covenants. This is the view of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They were called the two companions (al-qarinatan), and for this reason they were placed among the long (sevens) surahs."

He related this from ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan.

(p-337) The second: the basmalah is a guarantee of safety, and Bara'ah was revealed to cancel the guarantee of safety. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. It was revealed in the ninth year, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent it with ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) to recite it at the season of pilgrimage, after Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) had set out for the Hajj; Abu Bakr was the leader of the season. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None should convey on my behalf except a man from me." This is related by al-Hasan, Qatadah and Mujahid.

Al-Kalbi related that what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent from Surah al-Tawbah was the first ten verses of it.

Muqatil related that it was nine verses recited at the season, and ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) recited them on the Day of Sacrifice at the Jamrat al-ʿAqabah.

In His saying, ﴿A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger﴾, there are two meanings: the first is that it is the severing of protection from both of them. The second is that it is the expiry of their covenant.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾, and this is a guarantee of safety.

Regarding His saying: ﴿So travel freely in the land﴾, there are two meanings: the first is: go back into it to your livelihoods. The second is: travel in it wherever you wish.

Regarding al-siyahah (travelling freely), there are two meanings: the first is that it is walking at ease. The second is that it is going far away in fear.

They differed concerning to whom this guarantee of these four months was granted, into four opinions. The first: Allah, Exalted, made it a term for those whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had granted safety for less than four months, and for those whose term of safety was unlimited; after the four months, he is a combatant. As for one who has no guarantee, he is a combatant. This is said by Ibn Ishaq.

(p-338) The second: the four months are the guarantee of safety for the people of covenants; whoever's covenant was longer than them is reduced to them, and whoever's covenant was shorter than them is raised to them. Whoever had no covenant from the Messenger of Allah was granted safety for fifty nights from the Day of Sacrifice until the end of Muharram, because of His saying, Exalted: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak and Qatadah.

The third: the four months are a covenant for all polytheists, both those with a treaty and those without. This is said by al-Zuhri, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Mujahid.

The fourth: the four months are a covenant and guarantee for whoever had no covenant or guarantee from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). As for the people of covenants, they remain under their covenants until their terms expire. This is said by al-Kalbi.

They differed concerning the starting point of the four months, into three opinions. The first: its beginning is the Day of the Greater Hajj, which is the Day of Sacrifice, and its end is the expiry of the tenth of Rabi al-Akhir. This is said by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: it is Shawwal, Dhu al-Qaʿdah, Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram. This is said by al-Zuhri.

The third: its beginning is the twentieth day of Dhu al-Qaʿdah, and its end is the twentieth day of Rabi al-Awwal, because the Hajj in that year fell on that day; then in the second year it fell on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, due to what they had practised in the Jahiliyyah of intercalation (al-nasi'). The Prophet (ﷺ) confirmed it until the prohibition of intercalation was revealed, and he said: "Indeed time has returned to its form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth." ﴿And know that you cannot escape Allah﴾, meaning: you cannot outpace Him by fleeing, nor can you elude Him by seeking.

﴿And that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers﴾ may bear two meanings: the first: by the sword for those who wage war, and by the jizyah for those who seek safety. The second: in the Hereafter, by the Fire.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 3:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people﴾. Regarding the word adhan (proclamation) here there are three opinions. The first: that it means qasas (narration of news), and this is an opinion held uniquely by Sulayman ibn Musa al-Nashshabi.

The second: that it means a call to a matter that is heard by the ear; this was related by Ali ibn Isa.

The third: that it means notification (i'lam), and this is the view of the majority (al-kaffah).

And regarding ﴿the day of the greater Hajj﴾ there are three opinions. The first: that it is the Day of Arafah. This was said by Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn al-Musayyib, and Ata'.

Ibn Jurayj related from Muhammad ibn Qays ibn Makhramah that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delivered a sermon on the Day of Arafah and said: (This is the Day of the Greater Hajj)." The second: that it is the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), said by Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, and al-Nakha'i.

It was also related once from a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us upon his red she-camel and said: (Do you know what day this is? This is the Day of Sacrifice, and this is the Day of the Greater Hajj)." The third: that it refers to all the days of Hajj, so the day is used to express the days, said by Mujahid and Sufyan. Sufyan said: just as it is said "the Day of the Camel" and "the Day of Siffin," meaning all its days.

One opinion (on why it is called the greater): that it was so named because it was in a year when the Hajj of the Muslims and the polytheists coincided, and it also coincided with the festival of the Jews and Christians; this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that the greater Hajj is Qiran (combined Hajj) and the lesser is Ifrad (solo Hajj); this was said by Mujahid.

The third: that the greater Hajj is the Hajj itself and the lesser is the Umrah; this was said by Ata' and al-Sha'bi.(p-340)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 4–5:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed⦆ and so on.

Regarding "the sacred months" there are two opinions. The first: they are Rajab, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram, three consecutive months and one separate, and this is the view of the majority (al-jumhur).

The second: they are the four months that Allah the Exalted made a period in which they may travel freely and be secure, and they are: the twentieth of Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, Safar, the month of Rabi', and ten days of the month of Rabi' al-Akhir. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿And kill the polytheists wherever you find them⦆ has two opinions: the first is that it refers to (being) in the lawful territory (hill) or in the sacred precinct (haram).

The second is that it refers to the sacred months and to other than them.

Although the killing is in the form of a command, it is by way of choice (takhyir), since it comes after a prohibition, taking into account what is most beneficial (al-aslah).

﴿And seize them⦆ has two aspects. The first is in terms of advance and delay, and its sense is: "So seize the polytheists wherever you find them and kill them."

The second is that it stands in its own context without advance or delay, and its sense is: "Kill the polytheists wherever you find them, and seize them."

﴿And besiege them⦆ is by way of choice, in considering what is most beneficial of the two matters.

Regarding His saying ﴿And besiege them⦆ there are two aspects. The first: it means enslaving them. The second: it means ransom (fida') with property or exchange (shira').

(p-341) ﴿And sit in wait for them at every place of ambush⦆ has two aspects. The first: that they are pursued in every place, so that they are killed when found and pursued when they are far away.

The second: that everything that Allah the Exalted has prepared for them is done to them, in what He has ruled concerning them, of killing, enslavement, ransom, or release as a favour, so that the most beneficial of these is considered in acting.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But if they repent⦆, that is, they embrace Islam, because repentance from disbelief is by Islam.

﴿And establish the prayer⦆ has two aspects. The first: that is, they acknowledge its establishment, and this is what is implied by the saying of Abu Hanifa, because the one who abandons the prayer is not killed if he acknowledges it.

The second: that He intended the performance of the prayer, and this is what is implied by the saying of Malik and al-Shafi'i, because they both kill one who abandons the prayer even if he acknowledges it.

﴿And give the zakah⦆ means they acknowledge it in both respects together, because one who withholds zakah is not killed when he acknowledges it, and it is taken from his property by force; and this is a consensus (ijma').

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 6:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾ to the end of the verse. In the word of God there are two possibilities, meaning: if they seek safe conduct from you, then grant them safe conduct.

The first: He intended specifically the Surah of Bara'ah (Repudiation), so that it would make known what it contains of the ruling concerning the one who abides by the covenant, the ruling concerning the one who breaks it, the conduct toward the polytheists, and the distinction between them and the hypocrites.

The second: He means the whole Qur'an, so that by it he may be guided out of his misguidance and turn back from his disbelief.

﴿Then deliver him to his place of safety﴾ meaning: if he persists in polytheism and the period of safe conduct has expired.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not know﴾ this admits of two possibilities. The first: right guidance as opposed to error. The second: the permissibility of taking their lives once the period of their safe conduct has ended.(p-342)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How can there be a covenant with God and His Messenger for the polytheists?﴾ (Qur'an 9:7), the verse.

It admits of two interpretations. The first: when they have not been given safe-conduct (aman). The second: when they break faith and fight.

As for His saying: ﴿Except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾ (Qur'an 9:7), there are four opinions. The first: that they are a people from Banu Bakr ibn Kinana, related by Ibn Ishaq.

The second: that they are the Quraysh, which is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The third: that they are Khuza'a, related by Mujahid.

The fourth: that they are Banu Damra, related by al-Kalbi.

﴿So as long as they are true to you, be true to them﴾ (Qur'an 9:7). That is, so long as they remain upright in fulfilling the covenant, you should remain upright toward it. This indicates that when they breach the covenant, their safe-conduct falls away and their blood becomes lawful (to shed).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 8:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿How, when if they gain the upper hand over you﴾ means: if they become strong enough to be able to prevail over you.

In the speech there is an omitted element, and its estimated form is: "How can they have a covenant when, if they gain the upper hand over you...?"

﴿They do not observe toward you﴾ has two interpretations. The first: they do not fear, as stated by al-Suddi.

The second: they do not respect (or honour).

(p-343) ﴿Ill will, nor covenant (dhimma)﴾. Regarding "ill (il)" there are seven interpretations. The first: it is the covenant, which is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is the name of God Most High, said by Mujahid, and its meaning would be: they do not observe God regarding you.

The third: it is the oath (hilf), which is the view of Qatadah.

The fourth: "il" is the oath and "dhimma" is the covenant, said by Abu Ubayda. From this is the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

"The worst of people are the degenerate successors who left behind: they cut off the 'il' and the veins of kinship."

The fifth: it is the protection of a neighbour (jiwar), said by al-Hasan.

The sixth: it is kinship, said by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. From this is the verse of Hassan:

"I swear that your 'il' from Quraysh is like the 'il' of a young camel from the ostrich's brood."

The seventh: "il" is the covenant, the pact, the bond and the oath, and "dhimma" in this context is the observance of obligation toward one who has no covenant, said by some of the Basran scholars.

﴿And nor covenant (dhimma)﴾ has three interpretations. The first: protection of a neighbour (jiwar), said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: it is the observance of obligation toward one who has no covenant, said by some of the Basran scholars.

The third: it is the covenant, which is the view of Abu Ubayda.

﴿They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse﴾ admits of three interpretations. The first: they please you with their mouths in fulfilment of the covenant, but their hearts refuse except treachery.

The second: they please you with their mouths in obedience, but their hearts refuse except disobedience.

The third: they please you with their mouths in the promise of faith, but their hearts refuse except polytheism, because the Prophet (ﷺ) would not be pleased with the polytheists except by faith.

﴿And most of them are defiant (fasiqun)﴾ has two interpretations. The first: [they are defiant] in breaking the covenant, even though all of them are defiant by reason of polytheism.

(p-344) The second: most of them are defiant in their religion, even though all of their religion is defiance (fisq).

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿They have bartered away the signs of Allah for a small price﴾. Regarding the signs of Allah here, there are two interpretations. The first is that they are His proofs and evidences.

The second is that the signs of Allah are the Tawrah (the Torah, the scripture revealed to Moses) in which is the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The small price is what they substituted for that in place of it.

Regarding the description of the price as small, there are two interpretations. The first is that it is because it is unlawful, and the unlawful is small. The second is that it is because it is among the goods of this world, whose duration is brief.

Regarding those intended by this verse, there are two opinions. The first is that they are the Bedouin Arabs whom Abu Sufyan gathered at his food. This is the view of Mujahid and of those who hold that the signs are the proofs of Allah, exalted is He.

The second is that they are a people of the Jews who entered into the covenant and then turned back from it. This is the view of those who hold that the signs are the signs of the Torah.

﴿So they averted [others] from His path﴾ may bear three meanings. The first: from the religion of Allah, exalted is He, by preventing people from it. The second: from obedience to Allah in fulfilling the covenant. The third: from heading to the House of Allah when they were prevented at al-Hudaybiyah.

﴿Then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾. Concerning them there are three opinions. The first: that they are the chiefs of the polytheists. With a kasra, there are two meanings. The first: that they are disbelievers who have no faith (iman). The second: that they are not given any safe-conduct (aman).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 13–16:

His words, mighty and majestic be He: ﴿And they did not take, besides Allah and His Messenger and the believers, any intimate (wali'jah)﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions. The first: that it means betrayal; this is the view of Qatadah.

The second: that they are the inner circle (bitanah), this is the view of Qutrub and Muqatil, and from it is the verse of the poet:

The third: that it means entering into the allegiance of the polytheists, from their saying "Fulan walaja in such-and-such" when he entered into it. Tarafah ibn al-Abd said:

"I saw the rhymes slipping into hidden passages, [so narrow] that the needles can hardly pass through them."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 17–18:

His, may He be exalted and majestic, saying: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾, meaning the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram).

In this there are two interpretations. The first: it is not for them to maintain them while in disbelief, because the mosques of Allah, exalted is He, are maintained through faith.

The second: it is not for them to maintain it by visiting it and entering it.

﴿Bearing witness against themselves of disbelief﴾. In this there are three interpretations. The first: that what they say or do is evidence of their disbelief, just as their own acknowledgment indicates it, so that this from them is, as it were, their witnessing against themselves. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: it means bearing witness against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with disbelief, because they denied him and declared him a disbeliever, while he was one of themselves. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The third: when a Christian is asked, "What are you?" he says, "A Christian," and when a Jew is asked, he says, "A Jew," and a worshipper of idols says, "A polytheist." These were disbelievers even if they did not acknowledge their disbelief. This was said by al-Suddi.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah who believes in Allah﴾. Concerning these mosques there are two views. The first: they are the places of prostration within the prayer-place, and on this view, maintaining them may bear three meanings. The first: by guarding the establishment of prayer. The second: by abandoning showing-off (riya'). The third: by humility and turning away from what is forbidden.

The second view: they are the houses of Allah, exalted is He, built for the establishment of the prayers, and on this view, maintaining them may bear three meanings. The first: only the one who believes in Allah, exalted is He, maintains them through faith. The second: only the one who believes in Allah, exalted is He, maintains them by visiting them and praying in them. The third: only the one who believes in Allah, exalted is He, desires to maintain their building.

﴿and the Last Day, and establishes prayer, and gives zakat, and fears none but Allah. For those it is hoped that they will be among the guided﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: He said this to them as a warning against doing what contradicts their guidance. The second: every "perhaps" (`asa) from Allah is binding, even though from others it is an expression of hope. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 19–22:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque⁠ ﴾ — meaning by "its maintenance" the custodianship (al-sidana) of it and attending to it.

﴿Are they equal to one who believed in Allah and the Last Day and strove in the way of Allah? They are not equal in the sight of Allah﴾. This is because the Quraysh preferred that (act) over belief in Allah, so Allah, exalted is He, refuted them and informed them that the two are not equal, and that such (deeds) are nullified along with disbelief.

Muqatil related that this verse was revealed concerning al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who was the holder of the water-drawing (al-siqaya), and concerning Shayba ibn Uthman, who was the holder of the custodianship (al-sidana) and the chamberlain of the Ka'ba. Both were taken captive on the Day of Badr, and they were reproached for remaining in disbelief in Mecca, and the emigrants (al-Muhajirun) spoke harshly to them. They said, "We are better than you in reward: we maintain the Sacred Mosque, we guard the Ka'ba, and we give drink to the pilgrims." So this (verse) was revealed concerning them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 23–24:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your kinsfolk, and the wealth you have acquired⦆ means: the wealth you have earned (iqtaraftumuhā, "acquired" / "earned").

﴿and commerce whose slump you fear⦆. Concerning this there are two views. The first: that it refers to trade goods when their price falls and their market goes slack.

The second: that it refers to the unmarried daughters (al-ayama, "unmarried women") when they remain unmarried with their fathers and are not proposed for.

﴿and dwellings you are pleased with⦆. This was revealed concerning a people who embraced Islam in Makkah, remained there, and did not emigrate, out of concern for separation from what Allah the Exalted mentioned, inclining towards it and loving it. So Allah the Exalted blamed them for that and said: ﴿then wait until Allah brings His command⦆. Concerning this there are two views. The first: that it is the conquest of Makkah; this was said by Mujahid.

The second: "until Allah brings His command" refers to a punishment, either swift or delayed; this was said by al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 28–29:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day﴾. If it is said: the People of the Book have believed in Allah and the Last Day, so how does He say this about them? There are two answers to this.

One of them: their affirmation of the Last Day necessitates affirming all its rights, so by abandoning the affirmation of its rights they were like one who does not affirm it.

The second: He censured them with the censure of those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day, for their disbelief in His blessing, and in censure for disbelief they are like others.

﴿And do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden﴾. In this there are two aspects. One: that which Allah, glorified and exalted, commanded to be abrogated from their laws.

The second: what He made lawful for them and made unlawful for them.

﴿Nor do they follow the religion of truth﴾. The truth here is Allah, exalted is He. Regarding what is meant by His religion in this place, there are two views (p-351). One: acting upon what is in the Torah concerning following the Messenger, as said by al-Kalbi.

The second: entering the religion of Islam, because it abrogates the other religions, and this is the view of the majority.

﴿From among those who were given the Book﴾. In this there are two views. One: meaning from among the fathers of those who were given the Book.

The second: from among those who were given the Book in their midst, because in following him they are like their fathers.

﴿Until they give the jizyah﴾. In this there are two interpretations. One: until they guarantee the jizyah, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, because he holds that the jizyah is obligatory by the passing of a year and is taken along with it.

The second: until they pay the jizyah.

Regarding the jizyah there are two views. One: that it is among the ambiguous terms (asma' mujmalah), whose knowledge is not attained except through clarification.

The second: that it is among the general terms (asma' 'ammah) which must be applied in their generality except what is specified by evidence.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿out of hand﴾. In this there are four interpretations. One: out of wealth and capacity.

The second: that it is a gift for which no return is given, as said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

The third: that they see that for us, in taking it from them, there is a hand over them by preserving their blood through it.

The fourth: that they pay it with their own hands and do not have it delivered through their envoys, as the arrogant do.

﴿And they are humbled﴾. In this there are five sayings. One: that they should be standing while the one taking it is seated, as said by 'Ikrimah.

The second: that they should walk with it while they are unwilling, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that they should be humiliated and subdued, as said by al-Tabari.

(p-352) The fourth: that giving it is itself the humiliation.

The fifth: that the humiliation is that the rulings of Islam be applied to them, as said by al-Shafi'i.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 30–31:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And the Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah"﴾ — the verse.

As for the reason the Jews said this: when Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar) ruined Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), he burned the Torah until none of it remained in their hands, and they had not been memorising it in their hearts. So they grieved over its loss and asked Allah, exalted is He, to return it to them. Allah then cast it into the heart of Ezra, so he memorised it and recited it to them, and they recognised it. Because of this, they said he was the son of Allah.

Regarding who said this, there are three opinions. The first: that it was the saying of all of them, and this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: that it was the saying of a group among their predecessors. The third: that it was the saying of a group among those who lived in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Concerning these, there are two views. One is that it was Finhas alone; this is mentioned by ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn Jurayj. The other is that they were a group, namely Salam ibn Mushkim, Nuʿman ibn Abi Awfa, Shas ibn Qays and Malik ibn al-Sayf, and this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas.

If it is asked: if it was the saying of only some of them, why is it attributed to all of them? It is answered: because whoever did not say it at the time the Qur'an was revealed did not deny it, so it is attributed to them collectively, even though only some of them uttered it.

﴿And the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah"﴾ — and this is the saying of all of them. There are two views concerning the reason for their saying this. One: that when he was created without a male human father, they said, "He is the son of Allah," exalted is Allah above that. The second: that they said it on account of the one who raised him from the dead and healed the sick.

﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾ — the meaning of "that" is: although all sayings come from the mouths, it is a statement that is not accompanied by any evidence and is not supported by any proof, so it became a saying that does not go beyond the mouth, and therefore it was singled out with it.

﴿They imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them﴾ — i.e., they resemble. It is derived from their saying "imra'ah dahya'" (a woman who has not menstruated), likening her to men. From this is what came in the hadith: "The people most audacious against Allah, exalted is He, are those who imitate His creation," i.e., they are made to resemble Him.

Concerning whom they imitate, there are three opinions. The first: that their saying resembles the saying of the idol-worshippers about al-Lat, al-ʿUzza and Manat, and that the angels are the daughters of Allah; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada. The second: that the Christians' saying "The Messiah is the son of Allah" resembles the Jews' saying "Ezra is the son of Allah"; this was said by al-Tabari. The third: that in following their forefathers' tradition, they imitate the saying of those who came before them; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

﴿Allah fight them﴾ — concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: its meaning is "Allah curse them"; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, and from it is the saying of ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras:

*Qatalaha Allah, she blames me, though she knows that I am the one who ruins and reforms myself.*

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 32–33:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾. Regarding His light there are two opinions. The first: it is the Qur'an and Islam, as said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: it is His signs and proofs, because one is guided by them just as one is guided by lights.

He specified it as "with their mouths" because, as we have mentioned, no proof accompanies their speech.

﴿But Allah refuses except to perfect His light﴾. He does not mean its perfection from deficiency, because His light has always been perfect.

The intended meaning may carry two aspects. The first: the manifestation of His proofs.

The second: the aid of His supporters.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth﴾. It means Muhammad (ﷺ), whom Allah sent to His creation with guidance and the religion of truth.

Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: guidance is clarification, and the religion of truth is Islam, as said by al-Dahhak.

The second: guidance is the indicator (dalil), and the religion of truth is that which is indicated by it (al-madlul).

The third: its meaning is "with guidance toward the religion of truth."

The fourth: their meaning is one, and He combined them only for emphasis, given the difference in the two wordings.

﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾. Regarding this there are six interpretations. The first: it means at the descent of 'Isa, peace be upon him, for he will worship Allah, Exalted, only through Islam, as said by Abu Hurayrah.

The second: its meaning is that He teaches him the laws of the whole religion and makes him aware of it, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that He manifests its proofs and arguments, and Allah, Exalted, has indeed done that; this is the view of many scholars.

The fourth: that He makes it prevail in spite of the polytheists among its own people.

The fifth: that it was revealed on a specific occasion. The Quraysh had two journeys: the summer journey to al-Sham and the winter journey to Yemen and Iraq. When they embraced Islam, both journeys were cut off from them because of their opposition in religion. They mentioned this to the Prophet (ﷺ), so Allah, Exalted, revealed to him: ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾, meaning in the lands of the two journeys, and Allah, Exalted, indeed made it prevail there.

The sixth: that "prevail" means dominance, and the religion of Islam is the highest of all religions and the most numerous in its adherents. Allah has supported it through the righteous and the wicked, and the Muslim and the disbeliever. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas narrated from al-Hasan that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Allah supports this religion through people who have no share of the Hereafter."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 34–35:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿O you who believe, indeed many of the rabbis (ahbar) and the monks (ruhban) consume the wealth of people unjustly﴾ – the verse. There are two opinions regarding it. One: that it refers to taking bribes (rishw) in judgment; this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that it is general, referring to whoever takes it by any unlawful means.

He expressed taking by the word "consuming" (akl) because what they take of this wealth is the price of what they eat, and the term "eating" (akl) may be applied to the price of food, as the poet said:

Leave those who eat water, for I see that they gain no good after their eating of water.

That is, the price of water.

﴿And they bar (yasudduna) from the way of Allah﴾ may carry two meanings. One: that they prevented people from the truth in judgment by accepting bribes.

The second: that they prevented their own people from entering Islam by introducing doubt (shubhah) into their minds.

﴿And those who hoard (yaknizuna) gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah – give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾. Regarding this hoarding that deserves this threat, there are three opinions. The first: that hoarding is any wealth on which zakat is obligatory but whose zakat has not been paid, whether it is buried or not buried; this was said by Ibn Umar, al-Suddi, al-Shafi'i and al-Tabari.

The second: that hoarding is what exceeds four thousand dirhams, whether or not zakat has been paid from it (p-358); this was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, for he said: "Four thousand dirhams or less is provision (nafaqah), and what exceeds it is hoarding."

The third: that hoarding is the wealth that remains beyond one's need for it. Amr ibn Murrah narrated from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd who said: When the words of Allah the Exalted were revealed: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾ – the verse.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to gold and silver." He said: This was difficult for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: "Then what wealth should we acquire?" Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "I will find out for you." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, your Companions have been distressed and they say: 'Then what wealth should we acquire?'" He said: "A remembering tongue, a grateful heart, and a believing wife who helps one of you in his religion."

Qatadah narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Abu Umamah Suday ibn Ajlan, who said: A man from the People of the Bench (ahl al-Suffah) died, and a dinar was found in his loincloth. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A brand (kayyah)." Then another died, and two dinars were found in his loincloth. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Two brands (kayyatan)."

In the lexicon, kanz (hoard) is every thing gathered, some of it upon others, whether it is visible on the surface of the earth or buried in it, and from it comes the term "hoard of wheat" (kanz al-bur). The poet said:

May my lineage bring no good if I feed its guests the crumbled-barley-meal (qirf al-hatha), while wheat is hoarded (maknuz) with me.

Al-hatha: the sawiq (toasted flour) of the poor man.

He means: wheat is gathered with me.

If it is said: Allah the Exalted has said ﴿those who hoard gold and silver﴾, mentioning two kinds, then said ﴿and do not spend them﴾, and the pronoun refers to a single kind; and He did not say "and do not spend them both" so that the pronoun would refer to both.

To this there are two answers. One: the pronoun refers to the hoards (al-kunuz), and the sense is: "and do not spend the hoards in the way of Allah."

The second: He said this by being content with mentioning one of them instead of the other, since the context indicates that both share in it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they scatter toward it and leave you standing﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], and He did not say "toward them both," and as the poet said:

Indeed the prime of youth and black hair, if they do not disobey, is madness.

And he did not say "disobey both."

Then Allah the Exalted intensified the threat with what He mentioned after this: ﴿On the Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell and their foreheads, their sides and their backs will be branded with it: "This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard."﴾ He intensified this threat because of the nature of souls, which is stinginess with wealth, so that intensifying the threat would make it easier for them to pay it out in the rights (huquq) due.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 36:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months﴾ — meaning the months of the year. They were twelve months because they correspond to the phases of the new moon (al-ahilla), and because the sun and the moon descend into twelve zodiac constellations (burj), in which they move according to an agreed reckoning, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The sun and the moon [move] by a reckoning﴾ [al-Rahman: 5]. ﴿Of them, four are sacred﴾ — meaning that among the twelve months, four are sacred (ḥurum), that is, the sanctity of them (al-ḥurum) is the magnification of violating what is forbidden (al-mahārim) within them. This is what Sadaqah ibn Yasar narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delivered a sermon during the Farewell Pilgrimage at Mina, in the middle of the days of tashriq, and said: 'O people, indeed time has revolved and it is today in the same state as the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months, of which four are sacred: the first of them is Rajab of Mudar, between Jumada and Sha'ban, and Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram.'"

﴿That is the upright religion﴾ — it has two interpretations. The first: that is the correct reckoning and the complete count, as said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: it means the true, upright judgment, as said by al-Kalbi.

﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾ — concerning this there are four interpretations. The first: do not wrong yourselves by disobeying Allah the Exalted in all twelve months, as said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: do not wrong yourselves by disobeying Allah during the four months, as said by Qatadah.

The third: do not wrong yourselves during the four sacred months by making them lawful after Allah the Exalted has made them forbidden, as said by al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq.

The fourth: do not wrong yourselves therein, meaning do not leave off fighting your enemy during them, as said by Ibn Bahr.

If it is asked: why did He make some months greater in sanctity than others? It is said: so that restraining themselves from disobedience in them would be a means to continuing restraint in other months, a preparation of the soul to part with them, as a benefit from Him for His servants and as an act of kindness toward them.

(p-361) His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, the postponement (al-nasi') is an increase in disbelief﴾. As for al-nasi' in the months, it means postponing them, derived from the sale on credit (bay' al-nasi'ah), and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾, meaning, We postpone it.

Regarding the postponement of the months there are two opinions.

The first: they would postpone the year by eleven days until they made Muharram into Safar. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they would postpone the Hajj by one month every two years.

Mujahid said: So the Muslims performed Hajj in Dhu al-Hijjah for two years, then they performed it in Muharram for two years, then in Safar for two years, then in Dhu al-Qa'dah for two years. The second of these two was the Hajj of Abu Bakr, before the Hajj of the Prophet (ﷺ) the following year in Dhu al-Hijjah. This is when he (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, time has returned to its form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth." The one who announced the postponement at the gathering (al-mawsim) was from the Banu Kinanah, as related by Abu 'Ubaydah. Their poet 'Umayr ibn Qays said:

Are we not those who postpone over Ma'add, making the months of lawfulness into prohibited ones?

It was disputed who first postponed the months among them. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said: the first to postpone the months was Nu'aym ibn Tha'labah ibn al-Harith ibn Malik ibn Kinanah.

Ayyub ibn 'Umar al-Ghifari said: the first to postpone the months was al-Qalammas al-Akbar, who is 'Adi ibn 'Amir ibn Tha'labah ibn al-Harith ibn Malik ibn Kinanah. The last to postpone the months was Abu Thumamah Junadah ibn 'Awf, until this prohibition was revealed in the tenth year. He would proclaim: "I postpone the months every year." Indeed, Abu Thumamah was neither answered nor blamed. So Allah, glorified is He, prohibited postponement by this verse and made it an increase in disbelief.

(p-362) Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿so that they may match the number of what Allah has forbidden﴾, meaning, so that they may agree with it. So they forbade four months just as Allah, exalted is He, had forbidden four months.

﴿Their evil deeds were made attractive to them﴾. In this there are two views. The first: Allah, exalted is He, made them attractive by giving them fame and a distinguishing mark by which they might be avoided.

The second: their own selves and Satan made that attractive to them by embellishment and encouragement so that they would commit it. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Hasan.

As for ﴿their evil deeds﴾ here, there are two views. The first: it is what they had already done of making lawful what Allah had forbidden and forbidding what Allah had made lawful.

The second: it is showing off (riya'), said by Ja'far ibn Muhammad.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 38–39:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿O you who have believed, what is [wrong] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth?﴾ Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: They were called to the expedition of Tabuk, and they were sluggish, so this was revealed concerning them.

Regarding His words ﴿adhere heavily to the earth﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: [it means] clinging to residence in your land and your homeland.

The second: [it means] to the earth when it brought forth its fruit and crops. Mujahid said: They were called to that during the days of the ripening of the dates and the love of sitting in the shade.

The third: you became content with the worldly life, and He called it "earth" because it is in it. This is the saying of al-Dahhak.

This is clarified by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Are you satisfied with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ meaning, with the benefits of this world in exchange for the reward of the Hereafter.

The difference between contentment (al-ridā) and desire (al-irāda) is that contentment is for what has passed, while desire is for what is to come.

﴿Yet the enjoyment of the worldly life, compared with the Hereafter, is but little﴾ because this one ends and that one endures.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Unless you go forth﴾ meaning, in jihad.

﴿He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: The withholding of rain from them is the painful punishment with which you were threatened. It is also possible that by the painful punishment He intends that their enemies will overcome them.

﴿And will replace you with another people﴾ meaning, from among those who go forth when called and respond when commanded.

﴿And you will not harm Him at all﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: you will not harm Allah by abandoning the going forth; this is the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: you will not harm the Messenger, since Allah, the Exalted, has undertaken to support him; this is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

The third: you became content with the worldly life, and He called it "earth" because it is in it. This is the saying of al-Dahhak.

This is clarified by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Are you satisfied with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ meaning, with the benefits of this world in exchange for the reward of the Hereafter.

The difference between contentment (al-ridā) and desire (al-irāda) is that contentment is for what has passed, while desire is for what is to come.

﴿Yet the enjoyment of the worldly life, compared with the Hereafter, is but little﴾ because this one ends and that one endures.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Unless you go forth﴾ meaning, in jihad.

﴿He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: The withholding of rain from them is the painful punishment with which you were threatened. It is also possible that by the painful punishment He intends that their enemies will overcome them.

﴿And will replace you with another people﴾ meaning, from among those who go forth when called and respond when commanded.

﴿And you will not harm Him at all﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: you will not harm Allah by abandoning the going forth; this is the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: you will not harm the Messenger, since Allah, the Exalted, has undertaken to support him; this is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 40:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿If you do not help him, then Allah has already helped him﴾. He means: if you, O people, do not help the Prophet (ﷺ) by going out with him, and that was when he called you to go forth to Tabuk and you held back, then Allah has already helped him.

﴿When those who disbelieved expelled him﴾. He means from Makkah, and there was no one with him to defend him and protect him except Allah, the Exalted, so that He might show them by this that His help for His Prophet did not depend on them, such that their withdrawal and staying behind would harm him. Rather, it came from Allah, the Exalted, so their staying behind from him did not harm him.

In His words ﴿then Allah has already helped him﴾ there are two aspects. The first: by guiding him to the migration (hijrah) until He made him independent of their assistance. The second: by what He guaranteed him of support through His angels.

(p-364) ﴿The second of two﴾, that is, one of two. The Arabs have a usage in this, that they say "the fifth of five," meaning one of five.

﴿When they were both in the cave﴾. He means the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr, when they set out from Makkah and entered a cave in the mountain of Thawr so that they might remain hidden from those of Quraysh who went out seeking them.

The ghar (cave) is a depression in the mountain that one enters.

Mujahid said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained in the cave with Abu Bakr for three days." Al-Hasan said: "Allah placed at the entrance of the cave a thamamah, which is a small tree." Others said: "The spider was inspired and it spun a web over the entrance of the cave."

Some of those who delved deeply into the subtle meanings went to the view that His words, ﴿when they were both in the cave﴾, mean: in ghayrah (zeal) over what they saw of the manifestation of disbelief, so he was zealous for the religion of his Lord. This is contrary to what the majority hold.

﴿When he said to his companion, "Do not grieve"﴾. He means that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his companion Abu Bakr, "Do not grieve." His saying that to him may have two meanings. The first: that it was good news to Abu Bakr of victory, without any grief having appeared in him. The second: that grief had appeared in him, so he said that to him to lighten it and console him.

Grief is not fear; it is rather the heart's pain at what it imagines of the weakening of the religion after the Messenger. So the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: ﴿Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us﴾, that is, our helper against our enemies.

﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon him﴾. Concerning this there are two statements. The first: upon the Prophet (ﷺ), as al-Zajjaj said. The second: upon Abu Bakr, because Allah had informed His Prophet of the victory.

Concerning al-sakinah (tranquillity) there are four sayings. The first: that it is mercy, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that it is calm assurance, said by al-Dahhak. The third: that it is dignity, said by Qatadah. The fourth: that it is something by which Allah settles their hearts, said by al-Hasan and 'Ata'.

﴿And He supported him with armies you did not see﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects. The first: by the angels. The second: by trust in His promise and certainty in His victory.

Concerning His support (ta'yid) there are two aspects. The first: concealing his trace in the cave when he was sought. The second: preventing anyone from confronting him when he migrated.

﴿And He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾. It may have two meanings. The first: by the cutting off of their proof. The second: He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest by the humiliation of fear, while the word of Allah is the highest by the honour of victory.

﴿And the word of Allah is the highest﴾, by the manifestation of the proof.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾. Regarding this there are ten interpretations:

First: it means young and old. This was said by al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, and Mujahid.

Second: it means in ease and hardship, poor and rich. This was said by Abu Salih.

Third: it means occupied and unoccupied. This was said by al-Hakam.

Fourth: it means energetic and not energetic. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah.

Fifth: it means riding and on foot. This was said by Abu ʿAmr al-Awzaʿi.

Sixth: it means those with a craft and those without a craft. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Seventh: it means those with dependents and those without dependents. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

Eighth: it means healthy, unhealthy, and sick. This was said by Juwaybir.

(p-366) Ninth: it means according to the lightness and heaviness of the camel. This was said by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa and al-Tabari.

Tenth: light toward obedience and heavy against disobedience.

It may also bear an eleventh interpretation: light toward combat, and heavy in steadfastness.

﴿And strive with your wealth and your lives in the way of Allah﴾. As for jihad with one's person, it is among the collective obligations (fard al-kifaya, a duty that is discharged when sufficiently fulfilled by some), except when the enemy attacks, in which case it becomes an individual obligation (ʿayn).

As for jihad with wealth, it consists of providing its provisions and mount, if one is able to participate in jihad with one's person. If one is unable to do so in person, some scholars held that giving wealth becomes obligatory as a substitute for one's person. But the majority of them said it is not obligatory, because wealth in jihad follows the person, except the share allotted to the cause of Allah from zakat.

﴿That is better for you﴾. Regarding this there are two views: First, that jihad is better for you than abandoning it in favor of the permitted staying behind. Second, its meaning is that the good lies in jihad, not in abandoning it.

﴿If you know﴾. Regarding this there are two views: First, if you know the truth of Allah the Exalted in what He promised of reward and Paradise. Second, if you know that good lies in jihad.

It may bear a third view: if you know that Allah the Exalted wills good for you.

(p-367) His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿If it had been a near gain﴾, meaning: if what you were called to had been a near gain.

In this there are two views. The first: by "gain" is meant the matters that come easily, the things that present themselves with little effort.

The second: it means the spoils of war (ghanimah).

﴿And a journey of moderate length﴾, meaning: an easy and moderate journey.

﴿They would have followed you﴾, meaning: in going out with you.

﴿But the distance seemed long to them﴾. The shuqqah (distance) is a stretch of land whose traversal is burdensome for its traveller because of its remoteness.

﴿They will swear by Allah, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you."﴾ This admits of two meanings. The first: had we been able to leave our homelands and abandon our fruits.

The second: had we been able to find wealth to draw upon and provision with which to go out, we would have gone out with you on the journey to which they were called, but they held back from it, and that was the expedition to Tabuk.

Then, after that, they came swearing by what Allah reported about them, that had they been able they would have gone out, confirming His saying, Exalted is He, and validating the message of His Prophet ﷺ. ﴿They destroy themselves﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: they destroy themselves by the false oath. The second: they destroy themselves by holding back from answering the call.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 43–47:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words ﴿And had they intended to go out, they would have made preparation for it﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: the truth of resolve and the vigor of the soul. The second: provisions and mount for travel, and the maintenance of the family while at home.

﴿But Allah disliked their being sent forth, so He held them back﴾. He disliked their setting out only because failure would result from their unreliability, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and al-Jadd ibn Qays.

﴿And it was said, "Sit with those who sit"﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: "with those who sit without excuse," as said by al-Kalbi. The second: "with those who sit with an excuse, from among the women and children," as related by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

Concerning the speaker of this there are two opinions. The first: it was the Prophet (ﷺ), out of anger toward them, since he knew this about them. The second: it was the words of some of them to others.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words: ﴿If they had gone out among you, they would not have increased you except in confusion﴾. He means turmoil, as related by Ibn ʿIsa. The second: corruption, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

If it is asked: they were not in confusion, so how could these departing ones increase them in confusion?

It is said: this is from the disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), and its sense is: they would not have increased you in strength, but rather they would have caused confusion among you.

﴿And they would have hastened through your midst, seeking to cause you discord﴾. As for *al-iyda'* (ال­إيضاع), it is hastening in travel, and from it is the verse of the rajaz poet:

"Would that I were there as a trunk, I would race and hasten therein."

As for *al-khilal*, it derives from "passing through the rows" (takhallala al-sufuf), meaning the gaps that exist in them. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Align yourselves in the rows and let no one pass through between you, like the young of the devils (awlad al-hadhf)," meaning the devils. *Al-khilal* is corruption, and there are two views here: the first: they would have hastened in your corruption. The second: they would have sown discord among you.

Regarding the discord they seek there are two views: the first: disbelief. The second: division of word and fragmentation of the community.

﴿And among you are listeners for them﴾. Regarding them there are three statements: the first: among you are those who listen to their speech and obey them, as said by Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq. The second: among you are spies from your own people who convey your news to the polytheists, as said by al-Hasan.

﴿And do not put me to trial﴾ has three interpretations. The first: "Do not make me earn sin by disobeying in opposition." This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj.

The second: "Do not divert me from my occupation." This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The third: it was revealed concerning al-Jadd ibn Qays, who said, "Grant me permission and do not put me to trial with the daughters of the Banu al-Asfar, for I am known for my fondness of women." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 58–59:

The Almighty's words: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾, to the end of the verse. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: it refers to Tha'labah ibn Hatib, who used to say: "Muhammad only gives to whomever he wishes, and speaks with hypocrisy. If he is given, he is pleased, and if he is denied, he is angry." So this verse was revealed concerning him.

The second: what al-Zuhri narrated from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was distributing a portion, al-Khuwaysirah al-Tamimi came to him and said: 'Be just, O Messenger of Allah!' He said: '(Woe to you! Who would be just if I am not just?)' Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'O Messenger of Allah, permit me to strike off his neck.' He said: 'Leave him.'" Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾, to the end of the verse.

As for the meaning of yalmizuka (﴿finds fault with you﴾), there are three aspects. The first: it means that they seek to tempt you and ask you, as stated by Mujahid. The second: it means that they backbite you, as stated by Ibn Qutaybah. The third: it means that they blame you, as Ru'bah said:

"I brought my neck and my waist close together, in the shade of my age, with my falsehood and my blaming."

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-*ʿ*Uyun*) on surah 9, verse 60:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, the alms (*sadaqat*, zakat) are for the poor and the needy﴾. The people of knowledge (*ahl al-ʿilm*) differed concerning them in six opinions.

The first: the *faqir* (poor) is the one in need who abstains from asking, and the *miskin* (needy) is the one in need who asks. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Jabir, Ibn Zayd, al-Zuhri, Mujahid, and Zayd.

The second: the *faqir* is the one among the needy who is disabled (*dhu al-zamanah*), and the *miskin* is the one among them who is physically healthy. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: the *fuqara'* are the emigrants (*muhajirun*), and the *masakin* are other than the emigrants. This was said by al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim and Ibrahim.

The fourth: the *faqir* is from among the Muslims, and the *miskin* is from among the People of the Book. This was said by ʿIkrimah.

The fifth: the *faqir* is the one who has nothing, for need has broken his back (*faqar*), and the *miskin* is the one who has some property that does not suffice him, but he is content with it. This was said by al-Shafiʿi.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The *miskin* is not the one who has no property, but the *miskin* is the one with the *akhlaq al-kasb*." Ibn ʿUlayyah said: "*Al-akhlaq* (the worn-out, threadbare one) is, in our understanding, the *muhARif* (the one reduced to poverty through loss)." And the poet said:

*When he saw the feathers of the vultures scattered, he raised his primary feathers like the poor, disarmed one.*

The sixth: the *faqir* is the one who has some property that does not suffice him, and the *miskin* is the one who has nothing to be content with. This was said by Abu Hanifah.

Then He said: ﴿and those employed to collect them﴾, who are the collectors (*al-suʿat*) specifically entrusted with collecting and distributing them. The poet said:

*The collectors disobeyed you when you sent them, they did not do even a small thing (*fatil*) of what you commanded.*

The imam is not among those employed to collect them, nor is the governor of the province.

Concerning the amount of their share from them, there are two opinions. One: it is an eighth, since they are one of the eight categories. This was said by Mujahid and al-Dahhak. The second: it is the equivalent of the wages of their like. This was said by ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar.

﴿and those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾ (*al-muʾallafah qulubuhum*, those whose hearts are won over), who were people whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would win over with gifts. They are of two kinds: Muslims and polytheists.

As for the Muslims, they are of two types. One type whose intentions in Islam were weak, so winning them over strengthens their intentions, such as ʿUqbah ibn Zayd, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Aqraʿ ibn Habis, and al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas.

Another type among them whose intentions in Islam were good, but they were given in order to win over their tribes from among the polytheists, such as ʿAdi ibn Hatim.

Both types are given from the share of those whose hearts are to be reconciled.

As for the polytheists, they are of two types. One type who target the Muslims with harm, so they are won over with gifts to repel their harm, such as Amir ibn al-Tufayl. The other type who had an inclination toward Islam, and they were won over with gifts so that they would believe, such as Safwan ibn Umayyah.

Concerning winning them over after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with the designated share from the alms, there are two opinions. One: they are given it and won over by it. This was said by al-Hasan and a group. The second: they are prevented from it and it is not given to them, because Allah strengthened His religion beyond needing to win them over. This was said by Jabir. Both opinions are reported from al-Shafiʿi.

Hassan ibn ʿAtiyyah narrated, saying: ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said, when ʿUyaynah ibn Hisn came to him seeking from the share of those whose hearts are to be reconciled: "Allah has made you and your like independent."

﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills let him believe, and whoever wills let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. That is, there are no longer any whose hearts are to be reconciled today.

﴿and for the freeing of captives (*fi al-riqab*)﴾. Concerning them there are two opinions. One: they are the *mukatabun* (slaves contracted to buy their own freedom). This was said by ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Shafiʿi. The second: they are slaves who are bought with this share. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Malik.

﴿and the debtors (*al-gharimin*)﴾, who are those upon whom debt is due and who are obligated to pay it. If they incurred debt for their own needs, they are not given except with poverty. If they incurred debt for public interests, they are given whether rich or poor.

Concerning one who incurs debt in disobedience (*maʿsiyah*), there are three opinions. The first: he is not given, lest he be aided in disobedience. The second: he is given, because the obligation to pay has become due, and the disobedience has ended. The third: a penitent from it is given, and one who persists in it is not given.

﴿and in the way of Allah (*fi sabil Allah*)﴾: they are the warriors who fight in the way of Allah. They are given their share from zakat, whether rich or poor.

﴿and the wayfarer (*ibn al-sabil*)﴾. Concerning him there are two opinions. One: he is the traveler who does not find the means for his journey, and he is given from it even if he is wealthy in his own land. This is the opinion of the majority (*al-jumhur*). The second: he is the guest. This was related by Ibn al-Anbari.

The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And among them are those who hurt the Prophet and say, "He is an ear."﴾ That is, he lends his ear to everyone and listens to whatever anyone says. ʿAdi ibn Zayd said:

؎ O heart, find your consolation in something other than the body; indeed my concern is with hearing and with the ear.

﴿Say: "An ear of good for you."﴾ That is, he listens to what is good and acts upon it; he is not an ear of evil that acts upon whatever it hears.

Al-Kalbi said: This verse was revealed concerning a group of hypocrites who used to find fault with the Prophet (ﷺ) and say about him what was not permissible, so this verse was revealed concerning them.

There are two interpretations of it. The first: they would criticize him by saying that he is an ear that hears everything that is said to him, and they made this a defect in him.

The second: they found fault with him, and one of them said: "Stop, for I fear that it will reach him and he will punish us." Then they said: "He is an ear; if we answer him and swear to him, he will believe us." Thus they attributed to him acceptance of excuses regarding both truth and falsehood. This was said by al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

It was also said that the one who said this was Nufayl ibn al-Harith.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 62–63:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell﴾. There are three opinions regarding it:

First: "Whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger." This was said by al-Kalbi.

Second: "Transgressing its limits" (mujawazat hududiha). This was said by Ali ibn Isa.

Third: that it means opposing it (mu'adatuha), derived from hadid al-silah (iron of weapons), because it is used in hostility. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿For him is the fire of Hell﴾. This is a warning (wa'id). The fire was named Jahannam from the saying of the Arabs, "bi'r jihnam," when a well is very deep in its bottom (ba'idat al-qa'r). So the fire of the Hereafter was named Jahannam because of the depth of its bottom. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 64:

﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah may be revealed about them, informing them of what is in their hearts.﴾ [The verse begins with ﴿يَحْذَرُ المُنافِقُونَ﴾ and the rest of the verse is implied.] There are two views on it. The first is that it is a report from Allah Most High about their fear, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second is that it is a command from Allah Most High to them to be wary, and its implied meaning is: "Let the hypocrites be wary," said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding the words of Allah Most High, ﴿informing them of what is in their hearts﴾, there are two views. The first is what they concealed of hypocrisy.

The second is their saying during the expedition of Tabuk: "Does this man hope to conquer the palaces and fortresses of Syria? Far-fetched, far-fetched!"

So Allah Most High informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of what they had said, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

﴿Say: Mock[, then]﴾. This is a threat that takes the form of a command, for the purpose of warning.

﴿Indeed, Allah will expose what you fear﴾. It may carry two meanings. The first: He will make manifest what you conceal.

The second: He will give victory to those whom you forsake.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-*'*Uyun*) on Surah 9, verses 65–68:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾ admits of two interpretations. The first: some of them gather together with others in hypocrisy. The second: some of them take their hypocrisy from others.

Al-Kalbi said: "Some of them follow the religion of others."

﴿They enjoin what is evil and forbid what is good﴾. Regarding *al-munkar* (the evil) and *al-ma'ruf* (the good) there are two views. The first: *al-munkar* is everything the intellect rejects of shirk, and *al-ma'ruf* is everything the intellect recognizes as good. The second: *al-ma'ruf* in the whole Book of Allah the Exalted is faith, and *al-munkar* in the whole Book of Allah the Exalted is shirk. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

﴿And they withhold their hands﴾. Concerning this there are four views. The first: they withhold them from spending in the way of Allah the Exalted; this was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. The second: they withhold them from every good; this was said by Qatadah. The third: they withhold them from fighting alongside the Prophet (ﷺ); this was said by some of the later scholars. The fourth: they withhold their hands from raising them in supplication to Allah the Exalted.

﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾, meaning: they abandoned His command, so He abandoned His mercy toward them.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The hypocrites in Medina were three hundred men and one hundred and seventy women.

(p-380) Makhul narrated from Abu al-Darda', that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the description of the hypocrite. He said: "When he speaks, he lies; when he is entrusted, he betrays; when he promises, he breaks it; when he disputes, he transgresses; and when he makes a covenant, he violates it. He does not come to the prayer except late, and he does not remember Allah except a little."

Ibn 'Abbas said: The hypocrites in Medina were three hundred men and one hundred and seventy women.

(p-380) Makhul narrated from Abu al-Darda', that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the description of the hypocrite. He said: "When he speaks, he lies; when he is entrusted, he betrays; when he promises, he breaks it; when he disputes, he transgresses; and when he makes a covenant, he violates it. Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 69:

His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿So they enjoyed their share﴾ It is said: their portion of the good things of this world.

It may also mean their enjoyment by following their desires.

There is a third view: that it refers to their enjoyment of their religion, to which they persisted in clinging.

﴿And you plunged in as they plunged﴾ In this there are two views: the first is in the desires of this world; the second is in statements of disbelief.

Regarding who "they" are, there are two views: the first is that they are the Persians (Fars) and the Byzantines (al-Rum).

The second is that they are the Children of Israel (Bani Isra'il).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 70–72:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And goodly dwellings in Gardens of Eden﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

The first: the goodly dwellings are palaces built of pearls, red rubies and green emeralds (zabarjad), constructed with these jewels.

The second: they are the dwellings in which life is pleasant, and this is a possibility.

As for "Gardens of Eden" (jannat 'Adn), there are five views. The first: they are gardens of lasting abode and permanence. From this word the mine (ma'din) was so named because its jewel remains (iqamah) in it. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"If you seek hospitality from his forbearance, you will be hosted by one of weight who is firmly established (ʿadan)."

He means: one whose forbearance is steadfast.

This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the Gardens of Eden are gardens of vines and grapes in Syriac. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: 'Adn is the name of the innermost part (batnan) of the Garden, i.e., its middle. This was said by 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

The fourth: 'Adn is the name of a palace in the Garden. This was said by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Hasan.

The fifth: "The Garden of Eden is in the highest heaven; no one enters it except a prophet, a truthful one (siddiq), a martyr, or a just leader. And the Garden of Refuge (jannat al-ma'wa) is in the lowest heaven, where the souls of the believers take refuge." This was narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal in a marfu' report.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 73–74:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾. As for striving against the disbelievers, it is with the sword. As for striving against the hypocrites, there are three opinions concerning it. The first: striving against them with the hand; if one is unable, then with the tongue and the heart; if one is unable, then let him scowl in their faces. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: striving against them with the tongue, and striving against the disbelievers with the sword. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-383) The third: that striving against the disbelievers is with the sword, and striving against the hypocrites is by enforcing the prescribed punishments (hudud) upon them. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

They were the ones most frequently subject to the hudud.

﴿And be harsh with them﴾ may have two meanings. The first: hastening retribution against them. The second: not accepting their statements as true, and not fulfilling their oaths for them.

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying: ﴿They swear by Allah that they did not say [it]﴾. Concerning them there are three opinions. The first: that it refers to al-Jullas ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit, who said: "If what Muhammad brings is true, then we are worse than donkeys." Then he swore that he had not said it. This is the view of 'Urwah, Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq.

The second: that it refers to 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, who said: "If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it." This was said by Qatadah.

The third: that they were a group of hypocrites who said that. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿And they had already uttered the word of disbelief﴾: meaning what they denied of what we have previously mentioned, as confirmation of their lie concerning what they denied. It was also said that it is rather their saying that Muhammad is not a Prophet.

﴿And they disbelieved after their Islam﴾ may have two meanings. The first: they disbelieved in their hearts after they had professed faith with their mouths. The second: the ruling of disbelief applied to them after the ruling of faith had applied to them.

﴿And they planned what they could not attain﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions. The first: that the hypocrites planned to kill the one who denounced them. This was said by Mujahid. The second: that they planned what they had said: ﴿If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it﴾. This is the view of Qatadah. The third: that they planned to kill the Prophet (ﷺ). This is also related from Mujahid, and it was said that this occurred during the expedition of Tabuk.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 75–78:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and be among the righteous"﴾ (Qur'an 9:75), the verse and what follows it were revealed concerning Tha'labah ibn Hatib al-Ansari.

Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts:

The first: he had property in al-Sham (Syria), and he feared its loss, so he vowed to give charity from it. When it came to him, he was stingy with it. This is related by al-Kalbi.

The second: a mawla (freedman or client) of Umar killed a man belonging to Tha'labah, and he (Tha'labah) promised that if Allah brought the blood-money (diyah) to him, he would set aside Allah's due from it. When the blood-money reached him, he was stingy with Allah's due and did not set it aside. This is related by Muqatil.

It is also said: "When news of what was revealed concerning him reached Tha'labah, he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him to accept his charity. He said: (Allah, may He be exalted, has forbidden me to accept your charity.) So he began throwing dust on his head. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away, and he had not accepted anything from him."
