Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 79:

His words, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Those who find fault with the volunteers among the believers regarding charity, and those who find nothing but their effort [to give]﴾. It was recited with a damma and with a fatha on the jim, and there are two views concerning it. The first: their wording differs while their meaning agrees; this was said by the Basrans.

(p-385) The second: their meanings differ. Al-juhd with a damma means capacity (ṭāqah), and with a fatha means hardship (mashaqqah); this was said by some of the Kufans.

It was also said that this occurred at the expedition of Tabuk, and it was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, ʿAsim ibn ʿAdi, and Abu ʿAqil al-Aradi. The cause of this was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged giving charity so that he might equip [the army] for jihad. ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf came with four thousand dirhams and said, "This is half of my wealth as charity." ʿAsim ibn ʿAdi came with a hundred wasq of dates, and Abu ʿAqil came with a sa of dates and said, "I hired myself out for two sa, so I took one of them to my dependents and brought the other as charity." Some hypocrites who were present said, "As for ʿAbd al-Rahman and ʿAsim, they gave only to show off; and as for Abu ʿAqil's sa, Allah has no need of it." So this verse was revealed concerning them.

﴿So they mock them﴾. This may have two meanings: the first, that they showed their praise while concealing their blame; the second, that they were accused of showing off and openly mocked.

﴿Allah mocks them﴾. This may have two meanings: the first, that it is the recompense of mockers which He has imposed upon them; the second, that He has given them respite from being seized to account.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: This was at the time of the departure to the expedition of Tabuk.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 80:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them; even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will never forgive them﴾. This is in the manner of exaggerating the despair of forgiveness, even though it is in the form of a command. Its meaning is that if you sought forgiveness for them as one commanded to do so, or abstained from it as one forbidden from it, it would be the same in that Allah the Exalted does not forgive them.

His saying: ﴿If you ask forgiveness for them seventy times﴾ is not a limit for the occurrence of forgiveness after it. Rather, it is in the manner of exaggeration by mentioning this number, because the Arabs exaggerate with seven and seventy, since the middle of the decade, which is five, when one is added to it becomes the least degree of exaggeration, and when two are added to it becomes the greatest degree of exaggeration. Therefore they say of the lion "sabu'" (sabu' meaning "seven"), i.e., its strength has been multiplied seven times. This was mentioned by Ali ibn Isa.

Mujahid and Qatadah related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I will ask forgiveness for them more than seventy times." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them﴾, and so he refrained.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 81–82:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿The ones left behind rejoiced﴾, that is, those who were left behind (al-matrukun).

﴿in their sitting behind, contrary to the Messenger of Allah﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: it means opposing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is the view of the majority.

The second: its meaning is "after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," as said by Abu 'Ubaida, who recited in support:

"The abodes have been effaced after them, as if the palm-leaf weavers had spread a mat between them."

That is, after them.

﴿And they said, "Do not go forth in the heat."﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: this is what some of them said to others when they remained behind.

The second: they said it to the believers, so that they would remain behind with them. These were the ones left behind from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk, and they were eighty-four persons.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So let them laugh little﴾. This is a threat, even though it takes the form of a command. Regarding the little amount of their laughter there are two interpretations. The first: laughter in this world is little because of its abundant sorrows and worries, and their laughter in it is even less because of the threat that is directed at them.

The second: laughter in this world, even if it lasts until death, is little, because what passes away is little.

﴿And let them weep much﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: it refers to the Hereafter, because it is a day whose measure is fifty thousand years, and they will weep in it, so their weeping becomes much. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham.

The second: it refers to the Fire, forever, because when the punishment touches them they will weep from its pain. This is the view of al-Suddi.

It is possible that by laughter he means joy, and by weeping he means grief.

The second: meaning, before you sought permission.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 84:

His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾ "When ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul was on his deathbed, his son came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him to pray over him and to give him his shirt so that he could be shrouded in it. So he gave him the shirt, and he shrouded him in it and attended the burial. It was said that he [the Prophet] had reached him while he was still alive, so the Prophet ﷺ said: (The Jews have destroyed them). He [ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy] said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do not reproach me, and ask forgiveness for me.' When he died, [the Prophet] put his shirt on him and intended to pray over him, but ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, pulled him back and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, has Allah not forbidden you from praying over them?' He said: (O ʿUmar, my Lord gave me a choice, saying: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will never forgive them﴾. I will surely add to the seventy.) So he prayed over him.

Then it was revealed: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾, the verse. After that he did not pray over any hypocrite." This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Jabir and Qatadah.

(p-389) Anas ibn Malik said: He intended to pray over him, and Jibril took hold of his garment and said: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾ ﴿Nor stand at his grave﴾, meaning the standing of one who visits and asks forgiveness.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 85–87:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And let not their wealth nor their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in this world﴾. It admits of three meanings. The first: He punishes them by their preserving it in this world and by their anxiety over it.

The second: He punishes them by the calamities and misfortunes that befall them through it.

The third: He punishes them in the Hereafter for what they did with it in this world, at the time of earning it and at the time of spending it.

Ibn al-Anbari relates a fourth meaning: that it is according to inversion (al-taqdim wa al-ta'khir, transposition of words), and its sense is: "And let not their wealth and their children impress you in this world; Allah only intends to punish them through them in the Hereafter."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, [saying], "Believe in Allah"﴾. In this there are three meanings. The first: continue in belief in Allah.

The second: act as one who believes in Allah does.

The third: believe with your hearts as you have believed with your mouths, and this is an address to the hypocrites.

﴿But those of ability among them ask your permission, [O Muhammad], and say, "Leave us to be with those who sit [at home]"﴾ In this there are two meanings. One: they are the wealthy, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The second: they are those who have capability.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: It was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and al-Jadd ibn Qays.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They are content to be with those who remain behind [i.e., the women]﴾. In this there are three meanings: (p-390) The first: with the hypocrites, as said by Muqatil.

The second: that they are the lowest and most base of people, derived from the saying "Fulan khalafahu ahluhu" when he is among the lesser ones, as said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 90–93:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And those who make excuses among the Bedouins came, seeking permission to stay behind﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations (wajhan). The first: they are those who make genuine excuses, and they were excused for them. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, and it is the interpretation of the one who recited it with the light form (al-takhfif). The second: they are the negligent who make excuses with falsehood. This was said by al-Hasan, and it is the interpretation of the one who recited it with the doubled form (al-tashdid). For when it is recited lightly, it is derived from ʿudhr (excuse); when it is doubled, it is derived from taʿdhir (making excuses falsely). The difference between them is that ʿudhr is true, while ʿadhir (excuse-making) is false.

It was also said that they were the Banu Asad and Ghatafan.

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak nor upon the ill﴾, to the end of the verse.

Regarding "the weak" here there are three interpretations. The first: they are the young, because of the weakness of their bodies. The second: the insane, because of the weakness of their minds. The third: the blind, because of the weakness of their sight. Just as it was said in the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He, concerning Shuʿayb: ﴿And indeed, we see you as weak among us﴾ [Hud: 91], meaning blind.

﴿When they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾: regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: when they are free from hypocrisy. The second: when they take responsibility for guarding those left behind of the offspring and dwellings.

If it is taken according to the first interpretation, it refers to all of those previously mentioned among the weak and the ill, who do not find anything to spend.

If it is taken according to the second interpretation, it refers specifically to those who do not find anything to spend.

It was also said that it was revealed concerning ʿAʾidh ibn ʿAmr and ʿAbdullah ibn Mughaffal.

﴿Nor upon those who came to you that you might provide them mounts, and you said, "I cannot find anything to mount you on"﴾: regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: he did not find provisions for them, because they had asked for what they could take as provision. This was said by Anas ibn Malik. The second: he did not find sandals for them, because they had asked for sandals. This was said by al-Hasan.

Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said during this expedition, which was Tabuk: "Increase your sandals, for a man remains riding as long as he is wearing sandals."

Regarding those about whom it was revealed, there are five sayings. The first: concerning al-ʿIrbad ibn Sariyah, said by Yahya ibn Abi al-Mutaʿ. The second: concerning ʿAbdullah ibn al-Azraq and Abu Layla, said by al-Suddi. The third: concerning the Banu Muqarrin of Muzaynah, said by Mujahid. The fourth: concerning seven men from various tribes, said by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb. The fifth: concerning Abu Musa and his companions, said by al-Hasan.

(p-395) The Exalted and Majestic One says: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the emigrants and the helpers﴾. There are four opinions concerning them:

First: They are those who prayed towards both qiblahs (the two qiblahs, Jerusalem and the Ka'bah) with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

Second: They are those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the Pledge of al-Ridwan (the pledge of allegiance at al-Hudaybiyyah). This was said by al-Sha'bi and Ibn Sirin.

Third: They are the people of Badr. This was said by 'Ata'.

Fourth: They are the foremost, by death and martyrdom, from among the emigrants and the helpers. They preceded to the reward of Allah the Exalted and the goodness of His recompense.

It is also possible, as a fifth view, that the foremost, the first of the emigrants, are those who believed in Mecca before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated from them, and the foremost, the first of the helpers, are those who believed in the Messenger of Allah and his message before his emigration to them.

﴿And those who followed them in goodness﴾ may have two meanings: the first is in faith; the second is in good deeds.

﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

First: Allah is pleased with them for their faith, and they are pleased with Him for the reward. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Second: Allah is pleased with them for their worship, and they are pleased with Him for the recompense. This was related by 'Ali ibn 'Isa.

Third: Allah is pleased with them for their obedience to the Messenger (ﷺ), and they are pleased with Him for His acceptance.

(p-396) "And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Medina are those who have persisted in hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice; then they will be returned to a great punishment." [Al-Tawbah 9:101]

The saying of the Exalted and Majestic: "And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites" means: around him, that is, around Medina. Ibn 'Abbas said: Muzayna, Juhayna, Aslam, Ghifar and Ashja' — there were hypocrites among them after their conversion to Islam, just as there were among the Ansar, because all of them had come under (the Prophet's) power, so they were distinguished by hypocrisy even though obedience had encompassed them all.

"And among the people of Medina are those who have persisted in hypocrisy" (marradu 'ala al-nifaq). On this phrase there are three interpretations:

First: they persisted in it and did not repent from it. This was said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

Second: "marradu 'alayhi" means they were stubborn and defiant in it. From this is the saying of the Exalted and Majestic: "They invoke none but a rebellious (marid) devil" [al-Nisa' 4:117].

Third: they stripped themselves bare in it and openly displayed it, derived from "tajarrud khadd al-amrad" (the smoothness of a beardless youth's cheek) because of its clarity; and this is a possible reading.

"You do not know them" has two interpretations:

One: You do not know them until We inform you about them.

Two: You do not know the outcome of their affairs; We alone have exclusive knowledge of it. This prevents anyone from being judged as destined for Paradise or Hell.

"We will punish them twice" has four interpretations:

One: One of the two punishments is public disgrace in this world and the disapproval of the Muslims, and the other is the punishment of the grave. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-397) Second: one of them is the punishment of this world and the other is the punishment of the Hereafter. This was said by Qatadah.

Third: one of them is capture and the other is killing. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Fourth: one of them is the zakat taken from them and the other is the jihad to which they are commanded, because through their hypocrisy they regard that as a punishment. This was said by al-Hasan.

"Then they will be returned to a great punishment" has three interpretations: First: it is the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. Second: it is the enforcement of the prescribed penalties (hudud) in this world. Third: it is the taking of zakat from them.

(p. 398) The first: the righteous deed is jihad, and the evil is lagging behind from it. This was said by al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 106:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And others are deferred to the command of Allah﴾. They are the remaining three of the ten who lagged behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk and did not tie themselves to a pillar along with Abu Lubabah. They are Hilal ibn Umayyah, Murarah ibn al-Rabi', and Ka'b ibn Malik.

(p-400) ﴿Deferred to the command of Allah﴾: that is, delayed and held in suspense, awaiting whatever command of Allah the Exalted might come concerning them.

﴿Either He will punish them﴾: regarding this there are two views. The first: He will cause them to die in their present state; this was said by al-Suddi.

The second: He will order their punishment if He does not know their repentance to be sound.

﴿Or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾: this admits of two meanings. The first: that He knows the truthfulness of their repentance and so purifies what is in them.

The second: that He pardons them and overlooks their sins.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾: that is, All-Knowing of what their state will come to, All-Wise in what He did by deferring them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 107–108:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And those who took a mosque for harm and disbelief﴾. These were the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, and they were twelve men from the Ansar, hypocrites. It has also been said that they were Khidham ibn Khalid, and it was from his house that the Mosque of Discord (masjid al-shiqaq) was taken out; Tha'labah ibn Hatib, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, Abu Habibah ibn al-Az'ar, 'Abbad ibn Hunayf, brother of Sahl ibn Hunayf, Jariyah ibn 'Amir, and his two sons Mujammi' and Zayd, the two sons of Jariyah, Nabtal ibn al-Harith, Bijad ibn 'Uthman, Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, and Bahraj, who was the grandfather of 'Abd Allah ibn Hunayf. Concerning him the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you, O Bahraj, what did you intend by what I see?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I intended nothing but good," and he was lying, so he (the Prophet) affirmed him. So these men built the Mosque of Discord and Hypocrisy near the Mosque of Quba.

﴿For harm, disbelief, and causing division among the believers﴾: meaning, for harm, for disbelief in Allah, and to cause division among the believers, so that they would not all gather in the Mosque of Quba, whereby their word would be united, and so that they would disperse, whereby their word would be divided, and they would differ after having been united.

﴿And in preparation for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾. Regarding "preparation" (irsad) there are two meanings: the first is waiting for an expected evil; the second is guarding combined with action. Regarding "waging war against Allah and His Messenger" there are two meanings: the first is opposing them; the second is hostility toward them.

The intended addressee of this is Abu 'Amir al-Rahib, father of Hanzalah ibn al-Rahib, who had formed a faction against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then feared and fled to the Romans, adopted Christianity, and sought help from Heraclius against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). These men built this mosque for him, so that when he returned from Heraclius he might pray in it. They believed that if he prayed in it he would be victorious. They had begun its construction while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was setting out for Tabuk, so they asked him to pray for them in it. He said: "I am on a journey; if we return, Allah willing, we will come to you and pray for you in it." When he came back from Tabuk they came to him, having finished it, and they had prayed in it on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, and they said: "We have finished with it." Then news of the mosque reached him, and Allah the Exalted revealed concerning it what He revealed.

Muqatil related that the one who led them in prayer there was Mujammi' ibn Jariyah, who was a reciter of the Qur'an. Afterwards his Islam became good, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) sent him to Kufa to teach them the Qur'an, and he taught Ibn Mas'ud the remainder of the Qur'an.

﴿And they will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good"﴾. This may carry three meanings: the first: obedience to Allah the Exalted; the second: Paradise; the third: doing what is better, such as establishing the religion, the congregation, and the prayer, and this is an oath of scrupulousness.

﴿And Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars﴾. This may carry two meanings: the first: Allah knows that they are indeed liars in their words, deceivers in their faith; the second: Allah informs you that they are indeed liars and deceivers. Thus His informing him became like testimony from Him against them.

﴿Do not stand in it ever﴾: that is, do not pray in it ever, meaning the Mosque of Discord and Hypocrisy. "At that point the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched Malik ibn al-Dukhshum and 'Asim ibn 'Adi, and said: 'Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, and demolish it.'

So they went to it, took palm fronds, and burned it."

Ibn Jurayj said: rather, the mosque collapsed on Monday and was not burned.

﴿A mosque founded upon piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions: the first: it is the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina; this was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and he related it as a marfu' report. The second: it is the Mosque of Quba; this was said by al-Dahhak, and it is the first mosque built in Islam; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak. The third: it is every mosque built in Medina that was founded upon piety; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations: the first: from the mosque founded upon piety, there are men who love to purify themselves from sins, and Allah loves those who purify themselves from them through repentance; this was said by Abu al-'Aliyah. The second: in it are men who love to purify themselves from urine and excrement by washing with water (istinja'), and Allah loves those who purify themselves in that way. Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Anas ibn Malik related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Ansar at the revelation of this verse: "O assembly of the Ansar, Allah has praised you well concerning purification; what is this purification of yours?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we perform wudu' for prayer and bathe from major impurity." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is there anything besides that?" They said: "No, except that when one of us goes out to the privy he loves to cleanse himself with water." He said: "That is it, so hold fast to it."

The third: he meant those who purify themselves from having intercourse with women in their posteriors, and this is obscure; this was said by Mujahid.

His saying ﴿upon taqwa from Allah and approval﴾ may bear two meanings: (p-404) First, that taqwa is abstaining from His disobedience, and approval is performing His obedience.

Second, that taqwa is guarding against His punishment, and approval is seeking His reward.

ʿUmar ibn Shabbah used to apply His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Surely a mosque founded upon taqwa﴾ to the Mosque of Madinah, and he could take ﴿Is one who founded his building upon taqwa from Allah and approval﴾ to refer to the Mosque of Quba, thus distinguishing the intended meaning of the two in their respective places.

Second, that the site of the mosque, together with its structure and builders, fell into the fire of Hell. This was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

Second, that the doubt was at the time of its demolition.

Second, that it is remorse in their hearts, said by Hamzah.

It may bear a third meaning: that the doubt is fear of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and of the believers.

Second, unless they repent, said by Sufyan.

Third, unless their hearts are cut to pieces in their graves, said by ʿIkrimah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 111:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾. He purchased their lives through jihad (struggle in the way of Allah). ﴿And their properties﴾ may bear two meanings. One of them: their expenditure in jihad.

The second: their charity given to the poor.

﴿In return for that, they will have Paradise﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: meaning Paradise. This statement is a metaphor (majaz), its meaning being that Allah, exalted is He, commanded them to fight with their lives and their properties so that He would reward them with Paradise. He expressed this with the word "purchase" because it involves an exchange (iwad) and a counter-exchange (mu'awwad) that are both related to its meaning, and because the literal reality of purchase applies to what the buyer owns.

﴿They fight in the way of Allah﴾. This is because the reward for jihad is only deserved if it is done in obedience to Him and seeking His countenance.

﴿So they kill and are killed﴾. He means that Paradise is the return (iwad) for their jihad, whether they kill or are killed.

Jabir ibn Abdullah al-Ansari narrated that when this verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in the mosque, the people exclaimed "Allahu akbar." A man from the Ansar came, having folded the edge of his cloak over one of his shoulders, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, has this verse been revealed?" He said: "Yes." The Ansari said: "A profitable sale! We will not cancel it, nor will we seek its cancellation."

Some of the ascetics (zuhhad) said: Because He purchased perishable lives in exchange for the everlasting Paradise.

God Almighty says: ﴿The repentant﴾, meaning from sins.

It may also be that by them is meant those who turn back to God Most High, in doing what He commanded and avoiding what He forbade, because it is an intensive form (ṣīgha mubālagha) of praise. The one who repents (al-tāʾib) is the one who returns, and one who returns to obedience is better than one who returns from disobedience, because he combines both matters.

﴿The worshippers﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: those who worship by affirming the oneness of God Most High; this was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

(p-408) The second: those who worship by prolonging the prayer; this was said by al-Ḥasan.

The third: those who worship by obeying God Most High; this was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

﴿The praisers﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One: those who praise God Most High for the religion of Islam; this was said by al-Ḥasan.

The second: those who praise God Most High in ease and in hardship; this was narrated by Sahl ibn Kathīr.

﴿The travelers﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: the fighters (al-mujāhidūn). Abū Umāmah narrated that "a man asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission to travel (for worship), and he said: 'The travel of my community is jihad in the way of God.'" The second: the fasting ones (al-ṣāʾimūn); this is the view of Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās. Abū Hurayrah narrated it as a marfūʿ report from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The travel of my community is fasting."

The third: the emigrants (al-muhājirūn); this was said by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd.

The fourth: they are the seekers of knowledge; this was said by ʿIkrimah.

﴿The bowers and the prostrators﴾, meaning in prayer.

﴿Those who enjoin good﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One: by affirming the oneness (of God); this was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The second: by Islam.

﴿And those who forbid evil﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One: from polytheism (shirk); this was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The second: that they are those who did not forbid it until they themselves had ceased from it beforehand; this was said by al-Ḥasan.

﴿And those who keep the limits of God﴾. Regarding this there are three sayings. The first: those who uphold the command of God Most High.

The second: those who keep the obligations of God Most High concerning what He made lawful and unlawful; this was said by Qatādah.

The third: those who keep the condition of God in jihad; this was said by Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One: meaning those who affirm what God Most High has promised in these verses.

This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The second: those who act upon what God has urged in these verses; this one is closer to the view of al-Ḥasan.

The occasion of the revelation of this verse is what Ibn ʿAbbās narrated: "When the saying of God Most High was revealed: ﴿Indeed, God has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾ [9:111], up to the end of the verse, a man from the emigrants came and said: 'O Messenger of God, even if he commits adultery, even if he steals, even if he drinks wine?' So God Most High revealed: ﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers﴾ [9:112], up to the end of the verse."

The Exalted said: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they should be [close] relatives﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: what Masruq narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to the graveyard and we followed him. He came and sat by one of the graves and conversed with it for a long time, then he wept. So we wept at his weeping. Then he stood up, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) got up to him, and he (ﷺ) called him, then called us, and said: (What made you weep?) We said: We wept at your weeping. He said: (The grave where I sat is the grave of Aminah. I asked my Lord for permission to visit her, and He permitted me. I asked my Lord for permission to pray for forgiveness for her, and He did not permit me. And Allah revealed to me: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they should be [close] relatives﴾ — the verse.)

So I was seized by what a child feels for a parent. I had forbidden you from visiting graves, so visit them, for they remind you of the Hereafter.)"

The second: that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib narrated from his father, who said: "When death approached Abu Talib, the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon him, and with him were Abu Jahl and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah. He (ﷺ) said: O uncle, say, 'There is no god but Allah,' a word by which I may argue on your behalf before Allah. Abu Jahl and Abdullah ibn Umayyah said: Will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib? So the last thing he said to them was that he was upon the religion of Abd al-Muttalib. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: (I will indeed ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from you.) (So it was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾) — the verse."

The third: that it was revealed concerning what Abu al-Khalil narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) — (p-410) — who said: "I heard a man asking forgiveness for his two parents while they were polytheists. I said: Do you ask forgiveness for your two parents while they are polytheists? He said: Did not Ibrahim ask forgiveness for his father? I mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾."

The Exalted said: ﴿And the request for forgiveness by Ibrahim for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him﴾ — the verse.

Allah excused Ibrahim (peace be upon him) for asking forgiveness for his father despite his polytheism, because of the promise he had made earlier and his hope for his father's faith.

Regarding the promise for which he was asking forgiveness on his account, there are two opinions: the first is that his father promised him that if he asked forgiveness for him, he would believe. The second is that Ibrahim promised his father that he would ask forgiveness for him, since he was hoping that he would believe.

﴿But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah﴾ — and that was by his death upon his polytheism and Ibrahim's despair of his faith — ﴿he disowned him﴾, meaning he disowned his deeds and his asking forgiveness for him, so he did not ask forgiveness for him after his death.

﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was compassionate and forbearing﴾. Regarding this there are ten interpretations:

First: that the awwah (ʾawwāh, "one who laments much") means the one who supplicates much, i.e., who frequently makes supplication; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

Second: that it means the merciful; this was said by al-Hasan.

Third: that it means the certain one (al-muwqin); this was said by Ikrimah and 'Ata'.

Fourth: that it means the believer, in the language of Abyssinia (Habasha); this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Fifth: that it means the one who glorifies Allah (al-musabbih); this was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

Sixth: that it means the one who recites the Qur'an much; this is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Seventh: that it means the one who sighs (al-mutaʾawwih); this was said by Abu Dharr.

Eighth: that it means the jurist (faqih); this was said by Mujahid.

Ninth: that it means the one who is humbly submissive and humble (al-mutadarri' al-khashi'); narrated by 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Had from the Prophet (ﷺ). (p-411)

Tenth: that it means the one who, when he remembers his sins, asks forgiveness for them; this was said by Abu Ayyub.

The root of awwah is from ta'awwuh (ta'awwuh), which is grief (al-tawajju'), and from it is the saying of al-Muthaqqib al-'Abdi:

When I rise to saddle her at night, she sighs the sigh of a grieving man.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And Allah would not let a people go astray after He had guided them﴾ — the verse.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 117:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Certainly Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship﴾ — the verse.

This refers to the expedition of Tabuk, toward Syria. They were in hardship concerning the mounts, the riding animals: two or three men would share one camel. And they were in hardship concerning provisions. Qatadah said: "So much so that it has been related to us that two men would split a date between them, and a group would pass around a single date, each one sucking on it and then drinking water after it, and then the next one would suck on it." And they were in hardship concerning water, and they were under the scorching heat and its intensity.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAqil said: "One day they were struck by severe thirst, so they began to slaughter their camels and squeeze their stomachs and drink their water." ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "Then Allah sent rain from the sky by the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ), and it covered us."

Regarding this repentance from Allah toward the Prophet (ﷺ), the Emigrants and the Helpers, there are two possible meanings. The first: their rescue from the severity of hardship. The second: their deliverance from the harm of the enemy.

He expressed this by "repentance," although it departs from its usual usage, because the meaning of repentance (tawbah) is present in it, which is the return to the original state.

﴿After the hearts of a group of them had nearly inclined to deviate﴾ — in this there are two meanings. The first: they would be destroyed by the hardship and severity. The second: they would turn away from the truth in following and supporting [the Prophet], as stated by Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness; indeed He is Kind and Merciful to them﴾. This repentance is other than the first. Concerning it there are two views. The first: the first repentance was during the going forth, and the second repentance during the return. The second view: the first was during the journey, and the second after returning to Medina.

If it is said, according to the first view, that the second repentance was during the return, it may have two meanings. The first: it is the permission granted to them to return to Medina. The second: it is the aid given to them through rain falling upon them until they were revived. The repentance in these two meanings would then be general.

If it is said that the second repentance was after their return to Medina, it may have two meanings. The first: it is the pardon for them regarding the collusion of those who stayed behind from going out with them. The second: the forgiveness of what a group among them had intended of deviating from the truth. The repentance in these two meanings would then be specific.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 118–119:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And upon the three who were left behind﴾. It means: and He turned in mercy to the three who were left behind. In this there are two views. The first: they were "left behind" from repentance, and their acceptance was deferred until He turned to them. That is, [He turned] to the three who had not tied themselves to a pillar along with Abu Lubabah. This was said by al-Dahhak and Abu Malik.

The second: they were "left behind" from the expedition of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by Ikrimah.

These three were: Hilal ibn Umayyah, Murarah ibn al-Rabi', and Ka'b ibn Malik.

﴿Until, when the earth grew strait for them despite its vastness﴾, because the Muslims refrained from speaking to them.

﴿And their souls grew strait for them﴾, because of the estrangement they encountered from them.

﴿And they perceived that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him﴾. That is, they were certain that there was no refuge to which they could turn, for pardon from them and acceptance of their repentance, except Him.

﴿Then He turned to them in mercy﴾. Ka'b ibn Malik said: after fifty nights from the arrival of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the expedition of Tabuk.

﴿That they might repent﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that they might remain steadfast (liyastaqimu), because their repentance had already preceded, and He tested them with this for their own reform and the reform of others.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾. In this verse there are two views. The first: it concerns the People of the Book, and its interpretation is: O you who have believed among the Jews in Moses and among the Christians in Jesus, fear Allah regarding your belief in Muhammad (ﷺ), so believe in him, and be with the truthful, meaning with the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions in jihad against the polytheists. This was said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

(p-414) The second: it concerns the Muslims, and its interpretation is: O you who have believed among the Muslims, fear Allah. Regarding the intended meaning of this taqwa there are two views. The first: fear Allah from lying. Ibn Mas'ud said: "Lying is not fitting in earnest or in jest. Recite, if you wish: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾." And the reading of Ibn Mas'ud was thus: "min al-sadiqin" (from the truthful).

The second: fear Allah in obeying His Messenger when he commands you to fight his enemy.

﴿And be with the truthful﴾. Concerning them there are four sayings. The first: with Abu Bakr and Umar. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: with the three who were left behind, when they told the Prophet (ﷺ) the truth about their lagging behind and did not lie. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: with whoever is truthful in his speech, his intention, his deed, his inner state and his outward state. This was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: with the Muhajirun, because they did not hold back from jihad with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 118–119:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And upon the three who were left behind﴾. It means: and He turned in mercy to the three who were left behind. In this there are two views. The first: they were "left behind" from repentance, and their acceptance was deferred until He turned to them. That is, [He turned] to the three who had not tied themselves to a pillar along with Abu Lubabah. This was said by al-Dahhak and Abu Malik.

The second: they were "left behind" from the expedition of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by Ikrimah.

These three were: Hilal ibn Umayyah, Murarah ibn al-Rabi', and Ka'b ibn Malik.

﴿And their souls grew strait for them﴾, because of the estrangement they encountered from them.

﴿Then He turned to them in mercy﴾. Ka'b ibn Malik said: after fifty nights from the arrival of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the expedition of Tabuk.

(p-415) His words, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿It was not for the believers to go forth all together﴾. There are two interpretations of this.

The first: "It was not incumbent upon them to go forth all together, because its obligation had become one of sufficiency (fard al-kifayah), and this abrogates His words: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: its meaning is: "It was not for the believers, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ dispatched a detachment (sariyyah), that they should all go out with it and leave the Messenger of Allah ﷺ alone in Madinah until some of them remain with him." This was said by 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubaydullah ibn 'Umayr.

al-Kalbi said: The occasion of the revelation of this was that the Muslims, after being reproached for staying behind from the expedition of Tabuk, rushed to go out with the detachments of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and left him alone in Madinah, so this was revealed concerning them.

﴿Why should not a group from every section of them go forth, so that they may gain understanding of the religion﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: "So that the remaining group may gain understanding, either by being with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in his jihad, or by emigrating to him in his residence." This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: "So that the later group may gain understanding with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, after those who went forth on the detachments." The meaning of the statement would then be: "Would it not be better that, when they go forth, a group from every section of them remain, so that they may gain understanding of the religion with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" This was said by Mujahid.

Regarding His words ﴿so that they may gain understanding of the religion﴾ there are two interpretations:

The first: "So that they may gain understanding of the rulings of the religion and the markers of the Law, and bear from him what conveys the message, and warn their people when they return to them."

The second: "So that they may gain understanding from what they witness of Allah's support for His Messenger, His strengthening of His religion, the fulfilment of His promise, and the witnessing of His miracles, so that their faith may grow strong, and they may inform their people of it."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 123:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿O you who have believed, fight those adjacent to you of the disbelievers﴾. Regarding them there are four opinions:

First: they are the Romans (al-Rum), said by Ibn Umar.

Second: they are the Daylam, said by al-Hasan.

Third: they are the Arabs, said by Ibn Zayd.

Fourth: it is general in fighting the nearest, then the nearest, and then the next nearest, said by Qatada.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 124–125:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?"﴾ These are the hypocrites (al-munafiqun).

Regarding their saying that upon the descent of the surah there are two interpretations. The first: it is the saying of some of them to others in a manner of denial (inkar); this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: they say that to the weak among the Muslims in a manner of mockery (istihza').

﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith.﴾ In this there are two interpretations. The first: it has increased them in fear (khashyah); this was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The second: the surah increased them in faith because before its descent they had not been believers in it; this was said by al-Tabari.

﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ meaning doubt (shakk).

﴿It has increased them in filth upon their filth.﴾ In this there are three interpretations. The first: sin upon their sin; this was said by Muqatil.

The second: doubt upon their doubt; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The third: disbelief upon their disbelief; this was said by Qutrub.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verses 126–127:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested once or twice every year?﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Regarding the meaning of al-iftitan (being tested, put to trial) here, there are three views. The first: they are afflicted, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they go astray, said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

The third: they are tested (examined), said by Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.

As for that by which they are tested, there are four opinions. The first: it is hunger and drought, said by Mujahid.

The second: it is raiding and fighting in the way of Allah, said by Qatadah.

The third: it is the lies they fabricate against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman.

The fourth: it is what Allah, may He be exalted, reveals of tearing away their veils and the evil of their intentions, related by 'Ali ibn 'Isa.

And in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud it reads (Aw la taraa annahum yuftanun), addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 9, verse 128–129:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾. Regarding this there are two readings. The first: "min anfasikum" with a fatha on the fa', and its interpretation may be taken in three ways. The first: from among those most obedient to Allah, the Exalted. The second: from among those best in character. The third: from among those most noble in lineage.

The second reading: with a damma on the fa' (min anfusikum). Regarding its interpretation there are four ways. The first: meaning, from among the believers, one who has not been touched by any shirk; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ali. The second: meaning, from a marriage that did not touch him from the births of the Jahiliyyah (Age of Ignorance); this was said by Ja'far ibn Muhammad.

It has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "I came forth from a marriage and I did not come forth from fornication."

The third: from among those you know among yourselves; this was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: meaning, from all of the Arabs, for no branch of the Arab tribes remained except that they had given birth to him; this was said by al-Kalbi.

﴿Grievous to him is what you suffer﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: it is hard upon him that what troubles you should trouble you; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is hard upon him that you go astray; this was said by Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah. The third: "Grievous to him is the distress of your believer"; this was said by Qatadah.

﴿Desirous over you﴾: this was said by al-Hasan: desirous over you that you believe.

﴿To the believers he is kind and merciful﴾. Regarding this there are two meanings: (p-419) The first: by what he commands them of guidance and what he desires for them of righteousness. The second: by what he lifts from them of hardships and what he pardons them of lapses, and this is a possibility.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿But if they turn away﴾. Regarding this there are two meanings: The first: from the obedience of Allah; this was said by al-Hasan. The second: from you; this was mentioned by Ali ibn Isa.

﴿Say: Allah is sufficient for me; there is no deity except Him. Upon Him I have relied﴾. This may bear two meanings: The first: "Allah is sufficient for me" as one who helps me against you. The second: "Allah is sufficient for me" as one who guides you.

﴿And He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾. This may bear two meanings: The first: because of its vastness. The second: because of its majesty.

Yusuf ibn Mihran narrated from Ibn Abbas that the last of the Qur'an to be revealed was these two verses: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ and this verse.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: they are the most recent of the Qur'an in their bond with Allah. Muqatil said: their revelation preceded in Makkah, and Allah knows best.
